variants.title: Choose the interaction shape
variants.context: Choose the interaction shape before a protocol: request-response for one bounded result, asynchronous notification when a provider pushes after a durable change, a server stream for many ordered responses, a bidirectional session when both sides send.
variants.prompt: A dashboard in the browser only needs to receive an ordered stream of text updates and sends ordinary requests otherwise. Which shape?
options: Polling the update endpoint every second.
A server stream, such as Server-Sent Events.
A bidirectional WebSocket session per tab.
optionFeedback: Polling wastes requests when updates are frequent and still lags behind them.
One-way ordered delivery to the browser is what SSE is for, with event IDs and reconnection built in.
A full-duplex session adds connection state the product does not need.
variants.hint: Who sends, and how many messages?
variants.explanation: Pick the simplest live transport that fits. One-way server events do not need a bidirectional session.

variants.title: Choose the interaction shape
variants.context: Choose the interaction shape before a protocol: request-response for one bounded result, asynchronous notification when a provider pushes after a durable change, a server stream for many ordered responses, a bidirectional session when both sides send.
variants.prompt: A payment provider must tell your service when a charge settles, hours after the request. Which shape?
options: A request-response call that waits for settlement.
A bidirectional session held open for hours.
An asynchronous notification, such as a webhook.
optionFeedback: Holding a request open for hours is fragile and blocks the caller.
A long-lived session for a rare event is expensive state.
The provider pushes after a durable change; the consumer needs retry, deduplication, and replay rules.
variants.hint: When does the answer exist relative to the request?
variants.explanation: Asynchronous notification fits facts that arrive later. Design the delivery contract, not just the endpoint.

variants.title: Choose the interaction shape
variants.context: Choose the interaction shape before a protocol: request-response for one bounded result, asynchronous notification when a provider pushes after a durable change, a server stream for many ordered responses, a bidirectional session when both sides send.
variants.prompt: A collaborative editor needs both peers to send low-latency messages independently. Which shape?
options: A bidirectional session, such as WebSocket or gRPC.
Request-response calls with very short timeouts.
A server stream with a separate POST channel.
optionFeedback: Both sides send, so the channel needs identity, backpressure, heartbeats, and reconnect.
Request-response leaves the server unable to push when the other peer types.
The stream is one-way, so the two directions get different latency and no shared ordering.
variants.hint: Do both sides need to initiate messages?
variants.explanation: A bidirectional session is justified when both sides send independent events. Then the connection contract becomes part of the design.

variants.title: Use HTTP deliberately
variants.context: REST-oriented APIs expose resources through stable identifiers and standard HTTP semantics: identify the resource, choose method semantics, return HTTP evidence, and let intermediaries help.
variants.prompt: A product catalog API is being designed REST-style. Put the steps in order.

items.text: Let CDNs, browsers, and gateways help by preserving standard header meaning.
Return HTTP evidence: status, validators, cache controls, pagination, typed errors.
Identify a stable resource identity that does not leak storage layout.
Choose method semantics: safe and idempotent methods used accurately.

variants.hint: Resource identity comes before methods and headers.
variants.explanation: Identity → method semantics → HTTP evidence → intermediaries. Standard headers only help when the API preserves their meaning.

variants.title: Use HTTP deliberately
variants.context: REST-oriented APIs expose resources through stable identifiers and standard HTTP semantics: identify the resource, choose method semantics, return HTTP evidence, and let intermediaries help.
variants.prompt: An order endpoint returns personalized data. Put the steps in order.

items.text: Define conditional updates and repeated-write behavior for mutations.
Give the order a stable URI.
Return validators and Cache-Control that include authorization dimensions.
Make sure no intermediary caches personalized data under a shared key.

variants.hint: Cache identity must include everything that changes the response.
variants.explanation: Personalized responses need authorization in the cache identity, or intermediaries must not cache them.

variants.title: Use HTTP deliberately
variants.context: REST-oriented APIs expose resources through stable identifiers and standard HTTP semantics: identify the resource, choose method semantics, return HTTP evidence, and let intermediaries help.
variants.prompt: A team wants a CDN to cache public product pages. Put the steps in order.

items.text: Use GET for reads and define PUT or PATCH semantics for updates.
Confirm the CDN honours those headers and define invalidation in product terms.
Send Cache-Control, validators, and Vary consistently.
Expose products under stable identifiers.

variants.hint: Intermediaries help only when the evidence is right.
variants.explanation: Caching works when the origin states its promises with standard headers and the invalidation policy is defined in product terms, not only TTLs.

variants.title: Read the webhook contract
variants.context: A webhook 2xx means the consumer accepted delivery under the contract; it does not prove downstream actions completed. Providers retry transient failures with backoff and jitter and disable broken endpoints by policy; consumers claim the event ID durably.
variants.prompt: Your endpoint returns 200 for a webhook, then a later step in your pipeline fails. What did the 200 mean to the provider?
options: That you accepted delivery, not that downstream work finished.
That the whole business effect completed successfully.
Nothing, since providers ignore the response status code.
optionFeedback: Acknowledge promptly after durable acceptance; downstream work is your responsibility to retry.
The provider cannot see your pipeline, so a 200 can only report acceptance.
Status codes drive provider retries, and a 200 is what stops them.
variants.hint: What can the provider actually observe?
variants.explanation: A 2xx is an acceptance receipt. Persist the event first, then process; do not make the provider wait for downstream work.

variants.title: Read the webhook contract
variants.context: A webhook 2xx means the consumer accepted delivery under the contract; it does not prove downstream actions completed. Providers retry transient failures with backoff and jitter and disable broken endpoints by policy; consumers claim the event ID durably.
variants.prompt: The same webhook arrives twice after a provider retry. What prevents a double effect?
options: Claim the event ID durably before acting on it.
Compare the timestamps and ignore the older delivery.
Ask the provider to turn retries off for you.
optionFeedback: A durable claim on the event ID makes redelivery idempotent.
Retries can carry the same timestamp; identity is the stable signal.
Retries are part of the contract, and without them a lost delivery never arrives.
variants.hint: Which field is stable across retries?
variants.explanation: Consumers authenticate the signature, check replay age, claim the event ID durably, validate, and acknowledge.

variants.title: Read the webhook contract
variants.context: A webhook 2xx means the consumer accepted delivery under the contract; it does not prove downstream actions completed. Providers retry transient failures with backoff and jitter and disable broken endpoints by policy; consumers claim the event ID durably.
variants.prompt: A consumer endpoint has been failing for two days. What should the provider do?
options: Keep retrying every second until the endpoint recovers.
Drop the pending events silently and keep going.
Retry with backoff and jitter, then disable by policy.
optionFeedback: A one-second retry hammers a dead endpoint and hides the incident in noise.
Silent drops break the delivery contract and leave a gap the consumer cannot find.
Bounded retries plus a documented disable-and-replay path keep both sides honest.
variants.hint: What does a bounded retry policy need at the end?
variants.explanation: Providers expect broken endpoints. Disable by policy and let the consumer replay when repaired.

variants.title: Evolve without breaking
variants.context: Wire compatibility is necessary but not sufficient. Add, do not repurpose; deploy readers that tolerate both shapes; measure active consumers; retire with a plan.
variants.prompt: A field’s meaning must change. Put the evolution steps in order.

items.text: Measure client and schema versions, unknown fields, and deprecated operations by owner.
Publish timelines, provide tooling, test rollback, then remove old behavior.
Deploy consumers that read both shapes before producers emit the new form broadly.
Add a new optional field; never repurpose the old name or number.

variants.explanation: Add → read both → measure → retire. Changing a field’s meaning in place breaks clients that still trust the old one.

variants.title: Evolve without breaking
variants.context: Wire compatibility is necessary but not sufficient. Add, do not repurpose; deploy readers that tolerate both shapes; measure active consumers; retire with a plan.
variants.prompt: An enum gains a new value. Put the steps in order.

items.text: Retire the old handling only after evidence shows it is safe.
Roll out consumers that tolerate unknown values first.
Add the value without reusing any existing value.
Track which clients still fail on the new value.

variants.hint: A closed enum in an old client is a break waiting to happen.
variants.explanation: Consumers must tolerate values introduced by newer producers before those producers ship.

variants.title: Evolve without breaking
variants.context: Wire compatibility is necessary but not sufficient. Add, do not repurpose; deploy readers that tolerate both shapes; measure active consumers; retire with a plan.
variants.prompt: A deprecated operation must be removed. Put the steps in order.

items.text: Announce the sunset, help owners migrate, and remove it after the stated date.
Introduce the replacement operation alongside it.
Deploy clients that use the replacement.
Measure remaining traffic on the deprecated route by owner.

variants.hint: Removal is the last step, with evidence.
variants.explanation: Versioning is a controlled migration: replacement, adoption evidence, sunset policy, removal.

variants.title: Design the failure contract
variants.context: Every accepted interaction must have one defined meaning through success, timeout, retry, cancellation, and recovery. A timeout can mean never received, rejected, committed but lost, or still working.
variants.prompt: A POST to create a booking times out. The client library retries automatically. What is wrong?
options: Without an operation identity, the retry may create a second booking.
Nothing; timeouts always mean the request never arrived.
The client timeout is too short and should be raised.
optionFeedback: A timeout can mean committed-but-lost. Retry only with an idempotency key or operation ID.
A timeout is ambiguous by definition.
A longer timeout narrows the window but leaves committed-but-lost just as ambiguous.
variants.hint: What could have happened on the server before the timeout?
variants.explanation: Retrying state-changing operations because the transport timed out is a trap on every paradigm.

variants.title: Design the failure contract
variants.context: Every accepted interaction must have one defined meaning through success, timeout, retry, cancellation, and recovery. A timeout can mean never received, rejected, committed but lost, or still working.
variants.prompt: A public GraphQL endpoint accepts any query shape. Which control is missing?
options: Demand control: bounded lists, depth limits, and cost limits.
A faster database to absorb the expensive queries.
More resolvers so that each one does less work.
optionFeedback: Unrestricted queries let any client exhaust the service.
Capacity does not fix unbounded demand; one deep query can still ask for everything.
More resolvers widen the surface without bounding what a single query may ask for.
variants.hint: What bounds the work one request can request?
variants.explanation: Resource bounds are part of every paradigm’s production envelope.

variants.title: Design the failure contract
variants.context: Every accepted interaction must have one defined meaning through success, timeout, retry, cancellation, and recovery. A timeout can mean never received, rejected, committed but lost, or still working.
variants.prompt: A team picks gRPC because a blog ranked it fastest. What is the better basis?
options: Whatever framework the team most recently adopted.
The interaction shape, coupling, and delivery semantics.
Median latency measured in a small microbenchmark.
optionFeedback: Recency says nothing about whether this workload needs streaming or strict schemas.
No paradigm is universally faster; the workload decides whether its strengths matter.
A benchmark does not describe your failure contract or client coupling.
variants.hint: What questions must be answered before a protocol is chosen?
variants.explanation: Define interaction direction, operation identity, ordering, completion, and failure semantics first.
